cells.tense: The pen is in your hand and the thing you're tending is getting what it needs today.
cells.ask: Finish one thing all the way today — the last small step, not the next big one — and when it's done, take your hands off it.
cells.core:
You're carrying two things at once and neither one is falling down. You keep checking what each one actually needs — water, a rest, a firmer stake — and you give that instead of what would look impressive. What you care about reaches people mostly through the shape you give it, and the shape is holding.

What's working is that you know where your attention keeps going back to, so the daily decisions stop being arguments. Stay there by finishing one thing through and then setting it down — a good end, not a retreat. Tending can include stopping. When a thing is done, the setting-down is part of the work, not a failure of it.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what you love, and the shape is holding.
cells.place: where your attention keeps going back to

cells.tense: You're already standing in a harvest that hasn't come in, planning for a season that can't be written in yet.
cells.ask: Cut one plan down to the size of a life that can actually keep it, and do the small version today — no new equipment, no new people.
cells.core:
You're carrying a harvest that hasn't come in. Everything gets tended with tomorrow's version in mind — the one where it's already grown, already impressive, already sure. So the plans get bigger than the ground you're actually standing on, and care turns into grip. Watering harder doesn't make a seed open.

What you want is to stand in the finished thing now. It isn't here yet, and that's what not-here-yet means. Bring one plan back to the size of a life that can keep it, and do that small version today without adding anybody or anything to the load. Let the done thing be done before you dream the next one.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending a harvest that hasn't come in yet.

cells.tense: You once knew what you were pointed at, and now you're standing at a door that's already behind you.
cells.ask: Put ten minutes into the next small piece of one thing you used to care about — a page, a patch, a first line — and stop when the ten minutes are up.
cells.core:
You're not pointed anywhere right now, and the caring has gone quiet with it. There's a thing you used to put your hands on, and these days you don't, and the not-doing has started to look like having nothing left to give. It isn't that.

What went quiet is the habit of touching something small, not the care itself. Hope comes back by doing, so put ten minutes into one small piece of that thing — a page, a patch, a first line. Ten minutes, then stop, even if it's going well. Tomorrow, the same ten minutes. That's the whole instruction.
cells.sheetLine: The care isn't gone. The hands-on-it stopped.

cells.tense: You're already shaping what grows around you, and you talk about it as if it tended itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud who kept one thing alive through a hard stretch — start with yourself if that's true — and say it plainly to one person.
cells.core:
It's growing because you keep showing up — the small decision nobody watched, the picking of what's good for the thing instead of what's quick for you. You'd call that just how it goes. Somebody does it, and the somebody has been you.

The work is real and it's been getting no name, which is why it feels like effort with no floor under it. Give one piece of it a name out loud, to one person, and let them hear it. Naming it is allowed to be the finish line, not the start of more work. What you've held can be seen for what it is.
cells.sheetLine: You've been keeping it alive. That deserves to be said.

The sentence that serves me more than them is the 'twenty seconds' line — it is precision jewelry; I have cut it in favor of a finish a camera can see.
